name: Synthetic Monitoring and Real User Monitoring
intent: Know what users experience from two directions: scripted probes that test your site on a schedule from outside, and a browser SDK that reports what real visitors actually got.
scenario: At 03:00 UTC a regional CDN (content delivery network) problem makes the shop slow for users in Brazil only. Probes in Europe, the US and Tokyo keep passing. The browsers of Brazilian users report a p75 Largest Contentful Paint (LCP, the time until the main content shows; p75 means 3 in 4 loads are faster) of about 7 seconds, and that is how the problem is found.
problem: Your servers can look healthy while users suffer: a CDN edge, a DNS resolver, a third-party script or a mobile network is slow only for some people. Server metrics are measured inside your network, so they cannot see what the last mile does. You need a view from outside, and you need it both when nobody is using the site and when everybody is.

howItWorks.title: Synthetic monitoring: scripted probes on a schedule
howItWorks.text: A scheduler runs a script every 1, 5 or 15 minutes from several public locations: a plain HTTP check (status code, body text, TLS certificate expiry, DNS answer) or a multi-step browser journey driven by Playwright or similar (open the site, log in, add to cart, check out with a test account). Each run records pass or fail and timings. It works at 3 a.m. with zero visitors, gives a stable baseline you can compare day to day, and finds an outage before users do. It only tests the paths you scripted, from the places you chose to run it.

howItWorks.title: Real user monitoring: the browser reports back
howItWorks.text: A small JavaScript snippet (or a mobile SDK) uses the browser's PerformanceObserver and navigation timing to measure each page load, then sends a beacon with navigator.sendBeacon or fetch keepalive when the page is hidden. It reports Core Web Vitals (LCP for loading, INP for responsiveness, CLS for layout shift), JavaScript errors and resource timings, tagged with device, browser, country and network type. It shows the real distribution across every device and connection, but only for people who actually visited.

howItWorks.title: Read RUM data as percentiles, p75 for Web Vitals
howItWorks.text: A page-load time is a distribution with a long tail, so an average hides the people who suffer. Google assesses Web Vitals at the 75th percentile of page loads, split by mobile and desktop: LCP is good at 2.5 s or less and poor above 4 s, INP is good at 200 ms or less and poor above 500 ms, CLS is good at 0.1 or less and poor above 0.25. Segment by country and device before you trust a global number: a bad region is only a small part of the global p75.

howItWorks.title: Decide when a probe failure is an alert
howItWorks.text: One probe failing is usually the network between the probe and you, not your site. Probes therefore alert only when N of M locations fail in the same window (for example 2 of 3, 3 of 5), often after an immediate retry. A shorter interval finds outages sooner but multiplies single-probe blips; requiring several locations removes the blips but means a problem seen from only one location does not page anyone. The detection time you get is roughly the interval plus the time to confirm.

howItWorks.title: Alert on symptoms, and probe the critical journeys
howItWorks.text: Page on what users feel: the login journey fails, checkout takes more than 5 s, the Brazil p75 LCP is poor. Do not page on a CPU graph. Give the few flows that make money (login, search, checkout) their own canary journey with a dedicated test account and a cheap, reversible action such as an order that is cancelled or never charged. Everything else gets a basic uptime check.

howItWorks.title: Use each for what it is good at
howItWorks.text: Synthetic tells you quickly and reliably that something is broken at a place and in a flow you thought of, with no traffic needed. RUM tells you how bad it is for whom, including places and devices you never thought of, but needs enough traffic: at 1% sampling on a quiet night a country may produce too few samples to alert. Run both, link them to the same dashboards, and when a probe fails, use RUM to size the impact.

pros: Synthetic checks work with no traffic, so a 3 a.m. outage or a quiet new feature is still covered
Probes give a stable, comparable baseline and find outages before users report them
Probing from outside your network sees DNS, CDN, TLS and routing problems that server metrics cannot
RUM shows the real distribution by device, geography and network, including cases nobody scripted
Together they cover each other's blind spots: scripted paths and real behaviour
cons: Synthetic only tests what you scripted, from the locations you chose; a region without a probe is invisible
Browser journeys are brittle (a changed button breaks the script) and cost more than HTTP checks
RUM needs traffic, is noisy and is usually sampled, so quiet segments give too few samples to trust
Ad blockers and privacy settings drop RUM beacons, which biases the data toward users who do not block
RUM collects user data (IP address, URLs, user agent), which brings privacy and consent obligations
whenToUse: Any public website or API where users are somewhere you cannot see from your servers
Critical journeys such as login and checkout that must be proven to work at any hour
Sites that use a CDN, third-party scripts or several regions, where problems are local
When you need real performance numbers by country, device and network, for example to track Core Web Vitals
whenNotToUse: Internal batch jobs and back-end services with no browser or remote user: use server metrics, health checks and tracing
A small internal tool with a handful of users, where RUM samples are meaningless and one uptime check is enough
RUM as the only alarm for a low-traffic product: it cannot alert on a segment with no visitors
Browser journeys for every page: keep them for the few flows that earn money, they are slow and brittle
pitfalls: Running every probe from inside your own cloud or VPC, so DNS, CDN and public routing problems are never seen
Alerting when any single probe fails, which pages the team for every network blip (a 0.4% blip rate across 5 locations checking every minute is about 29 failed checks a day)
Requiring N of M locations without noticing that a regional fault only fails one location, so the rule hides exactly the regional outage you wanted to catch
Probes that always fetch the same cached URL with the same warm cookie, so they never exercise the slow path real users hit
Test accounts and synthetic orders that pollute analytics, trigger real emails or charge real cards; tag the traffic and exclude it
Reading RUM averages or a global p75 only, so a bad country hides inside a healthy total
Putting the RUM endpoint on a third-party domain that ad blockers list, and then trusting the numbers (serve it first-party)
Collecting full URLs with tokens or IP addresses in the beacon, and sending RUM before consent where the law requires it
A probe that runs in the same region as the monitoring backend, or no alert if the probes themselves stop running

quiz.question: At 03:00 UTC a CDN fault makes the shop slow for users in Brazil only. Scripted probes in Europe, the US and Tokyo stay green, but real browsers in Brazil report a p75 LCP of 7 seconds. Why did the probes miss it?
options: Probes cannot measure page load time at all, only status codes
The probe interval of 5 minutes was simply too long
None of the probes ran from Brazil
The probes skip the CDN and always go straight to the origin
quiz.explanation: Synthetic checks cover only the paths and places you scripted, so a regional fault elsewhere is invisible. Real user monitoring measures where users actually are. A shorter interval would not help, because no probe was in the affected region.

quiz.question: Five probe locations check the login page every minute. The team pages on any single failed check and gets about 20 pages a day, nearly all one location failing once. The goal is to page for outages that affect users broadly. What is the best change?
options: Alert only when all 5 locations fail at the same moment
Check every 15 minutes instead of every minute, to cut noise
Alert when 2 of 5 locations fail together, after one retry
Add 15 more probe locations so every blip is confirmed
quiz.explanation: A single failing probe is usually the path between that probe and you. Requiring several locations to agree, after a retry, removes the blips and still catches broad outages. Requiring all 5 misses partial outages, and more locations means more blips.

quiz.question: A shop's global p75 LCP is 2.3 s, which is rated good, yet mobile users in Brazil, about 2% of traffic, complain about slow pages. What should the team change in how it uses RUM data?
options: Track and alert on p75 per country and device
Lower the global p75 alert threshold to 2.0 s so it fires sooner
Switch from p75 to the average, which reacts faster to change
Raise sampling to 100% and keep one global figure
quiz.explanation: A bad segment of 2% barely moves a global percentile, so it hides inside a healthy total. Splitting by country and device exposes it. The average hides tails even more, and higher sampling still feeds the same blended number.
